title: Modi Asked Indians to Stop Buying Gold. The NSE Just Built a Way to Own It Without Touching It.
excerpt: Electronic Gold Receipts let investors hold real physical gold in digital form through their demat accounts. With 50,000 tonnes sitting idle in Indian households and temples, the country is trying to unlock the world's largest private gold reserve.
body:
India imports roughly 700 tonnes of gold every year. It is the country's second-largest import bill after crude oil, and in a year when Brent is flirting with $97 a barrel and the rupee is Asia's worst-performing major currency, every tonne of imported gold adds direct pressure to the current account deficit. Prime Minister Narendra Modi recently made an unusual public appeal: stop buying gold for a year.

The National Stock Exchange had a different idea. On May 4, it launched Electronic Gold Receipts — a new financial instrument that lets investors own physical gold in digital form through their demat accounts, without ever touching, storing, or insuring a single gram themselves.

## What EGRs Actually Are

An Electronic Gold Receipt is a digital certificate representing ownership of a specific quantity of physical gold stored in a SEBI-approved vault. Each EGR is backed by real metal — not a promise, not a derivative, not a fund manager's judgment call. The gold must meet the purity standards set by both the London Bullion Market Association and the Bureau of Indian Standards before it can be converted into an EGR.

"The introduction of EGRs at NSE marks a pivotal evolution in how India interacts with its most cherished asset," said Sriram Krishnan, Chief Business Development Officer at NSE. The exchange publicly dematerialised a 1,000-gram gold bar into an EGR at launch, demonstrating the seamless conversion between physical and digital formats.

The timing, Krishnan clarified, was coincidental — not a response to Modi's gold boycott call. "This was a planned launch anyway. We wanted to reduce the import of gold through the EGR concept," he told ANI. But both efforts share the same objective: reducing India's dependence on gold imports by channelling existing domestic gold into the formal financial system.

## How They Differ From Gold ETFs

India already has Gold ETFs, so why build another digital gold product? The differences are substantive.

A Gold ETF is a unit in a fund that invests in gold. You own a share of the fund, not the metal itself. You cannot take delivery of the physical gold. An EGR, by contrast, represents direct ownership of specific gold stored in a specific vault. Holders can convert their EGRs back into physical gold if they choose. This makes EGRs fundamentally different — they are not a financial product layered on top of gold. They *are* gold, held in digital form.

For retail investors, EGRs also offer fractional ownership. You do not need to buy a full kilogram bar. Smaller denominations are available, making it accessible as a portfolio diversifier for anyone with a demat account.

The security advantages are straightforward: no theft risk, no storage costs, no purity concerns, no bank locker fees. The gold sits in a regulated vault. Your ownership sits in your demat account. And unlike jewellery, which loses 15 to 25 per cent of its value to making charges the moment you buy it, EGRs trade at market price with transparent price discovery on the exchange.

## The 50,000-Tonne Opportunity

The real ambition behind EGRs is not retail investment. It is the staggering 50,000 tonnes of gold estimated to be sitting in Indian households and temples — worth roughly $11 trillion at current prices. This is the world's largest private gold reserve, and almost none of it participates in the financial system.

Krishnan estimated that 100 to 200 tonnes could be converted into EGRs in the first year alone. "India imports about 700 tonnes of gold every year. If what we are seeing comes true, then about 100 to 200 tonnes of imports can be avoided," he said.

If successful, the platform could position India as a genuine price-maker in global gold markets rather than a price-taker. "One single market for the whole country" is how Krishnan described the vision — a unified, transparent, exchange-traded gold market that brings the informal into the formal.

## What NRIs Need to Know

For the diaspora, the implications are layered. Gold remains the most culturally significant asset class for Indian families abroad. NRIs buy gold for weddings, for newborns, for Diwali, and as a hedge against currency risk in both directions. Many send gold back to India or ask family members to buy on their behalf, adding logistics, trust, and customs complications to every transaction.

EGRs potentially simplify all of this. If NRIs can access EGRs through their NRE or NRO-linked demat accounts — the regulatory framework for which is still evolving — they could hold Indian-vaulted physical gold digitally from anywhere in the world. No shipping. No customs declarations. No worrying about a relative's locker.

The product is expected to appear on major brokerage platforms within two to three months. The early response from institutional stakeholders has been, in Krishnan's words, "overwhelming."

For a country where gold is not just an investment but an emotional inheritance, the EGR represents something rare in Indian finance: an instrument that respects tradition while modernising the plumbing underneath it. Whether NRIs and domestic investors actually embrace it will depend on trust, accessibility, and whether India's brokerage ecosystem delivers the kind of frictionless experience that a demat gold product demands.

Gold at $4,335 an ounce is no longer a passive heirloom. It is a strategic asset. The question is whether India can finally treat it like one.
